cards.title: The Lightbulb Computer

depth.text: someone imagined a **lightbulb-shaped projector** that puts **useful information** onto surfaces around the home

The demos use a **real but bulky setup**: a Mac with custom software, a small consumer **4k laser projector**, and a basic webcam. The author says the technology isn't quite ready for a consumer version.

cards.camps: Two camps: some like the shared, more natural interactions; others worry about a machine constantly present and watching at home.

comments.text: I made this, fun to see my project on the front page! The main question I tend to get from hacker-types is "what are the tech specs?". The demos run on a Mac with custom software I built for projection mapping/rendering/etc. (the hand tracking uses Apple's built-in framework, which is very good), a small consumer 4k laser projector, and a basic webcam for vision. But really, this is primarily a…

Really some good thinking here. We need these awesome ideas to escape from the screens, which I call as blackholes of attention. However, the light bulb concept is limited to indoor usecases - which is not bad - that's where people live most of the time. The broader goal should be to get rid of dependency on screens, technologies and information. That's when AI can stop enslaving us with HITL etc.

Nice. This reminds me how I felt watching the first pre-iPhone multitouch demos. One small quality-of-life improvement that could be added: have the software timestamp when you say "here" and then (using a short low-FPS video buffer?) analyze the corresponding frame of video. This would eliminate the pause when you're pointing at something, waiting for the computer to respond. Alternately a…
Oh my god!!! I was working towards this exact thing for the last 7+ years. Albeit from a home IoT smart speaker angle. So glad to see this!!

Quite nice. But this imbues the house with a constant presence of the machine. A jinn which is always ready to grant your wish, but never leaves you alone, ever watching and listening. The fact that the jinn takes orders spoken in normal human language amplifies the effect quite a bit. I would have rather not have to feel such presence in my bathroom. Or bedroom. I would still be glad to be able…

cards.title: Build your own decision model

depth.text: someone made a language model **pick fixed answers** and tried to make its **confidence** match reality

The author constrains **Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B** to answers A–E; on a random sample holdout of CommonsenseQA, macro F1 rose from **0.5844 to 0.6234** after fine-tuning. They then use **temperature scaling** to adjust the probability scores toward the model's accuracy.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say Jev is just a classifier with a new name; others like the approach and see more potential in it.

comments.text: So "decision model" is the new cool term for classifiers? You know, that thing that already existed decades ago
Just for the author: On any of my iOS 26 browsers (orion, brave, safari), a page reload occurs when the model download completes, which resets the state, so I never get to interact with the model.

This is a great way to start but the perf of LLM models like Qwen are not ideal for local execution. I have adapted Laya (pure decision model) to run in a browser and I am able to get responses under 200ms. Give it a try: https://wexare-ai.github.io/browser-laya/

I saw Jev and without understanding it said to myself, “I can build that!” And brainstormed some weird Alex trebek jeopardy generator I called trebek, a bun ran typescript app that you give it an input, it decides if it’s a category, question or answer then generates what’s missing. Trained a SQLite-vec database on the English language for a few days with a small qwen embedding model to add vec…

What if Jev is something more than a classifier? There's so much potential here waiting to be seen. I built my own Jev, then realized it could literally run on a webpage. So then I turned it into an npm library https://genclass.dev

depth.text: someone found **DuckDB reads data from S3** much faster, without changing the query

For a query reading one column from a 2.2 GB Parquet file, the writer’s M5 laptop took **18.8 s** with DuckDB 1.5.5 and **7.7 s** with the 2.0 alpha. A separate pool of download threads fetches row groups ahead, so workers can decode while downloads continue.
data: One 2.2 GB Parquet file, one column — DuckDB 1.5.5
One 2.2 GB Parquet file, one column — DuckDB 2.0 alpha

comments.text: Great visualization. Side note their new c++ extension api is also gonna be faster from the perspective of development / distribution of those extensions

Nice article! While it's true that 2.0 makes recursive CTEs much more performant, don't forget that there's a badass DuckDB extension for graph data already. Here's a 2025 article about how elegantly that can handle what is otherwise quite a challenging class of query for your typical RDBMS: https://duckdb.org/2025/10/22/duckdb-graph-queries-duckpgq

I wish more database engines used a Task-based design like Umbra / CedarDB. Most of the DB engines out there still seem to use a "n-threads" style parallelism with exchange operations and poor async I/O management. DuckDB is improving on this front, but in some sense is catching up to R&D (and implementation!) that is now decades old. A "rhetorical challenge" I like to give software developers…
Going to try it out in my next jupyter notebook.

I was ok with the AI writing until I got to the fact that they added Triggers in 2.0 and the article decided that was meh compared to optimizing workers for S3 file access on slow connections. Nope. I'll read the release notes myself.

cards.title: Knuth reward check

depth.text: someone found an **error** on page one of a Donald Knuth book and earned his **reward check**

The error was in the first word of **Computer Modern Typefaces**; one commenter says it claimed **“infinitely many alphabets can be generated”** despite only finitely many possible settings. The first check was **$2.88**, and a later wrong report still earned $0.32.

cards.camps: Two camps: some suggest using AI to find more errors in Knuth’s books; others say not to, warning it would kill an amazing thing.

comments.text: The biggest shame of my life is that I had one of these and somehow managed to lose it.

The error was saying that "infinitely many alphabets can be generated" but there is a finite number of parameters which have a finite range of values. If Knuth had just written "a humongous number of alphabets" he would be correct.
It's not a reward check, but Knuth read one of my articles and emailed me about it [0], which I found pretty cool. [0]: https://tug.org/TUGboat/tb43-3/tb135chernoff-lwc.pdf

It was a bit more than 25 years ago for me, check #790 for $2.88 DT 33, (143). Really need to find another error or point of improvement so as to get the digital account --- I've been reading through TAoCP Vol. 4 Fascicle 7 on _Constraint Satisfaction_, but it's been slow going (though I did find out that it is intentional that he not list beginning of chapter quotes in the index).

I wondered how you received a real check since Knuth has not been sending out real checks (as you have noted) for some time now, only to see that you explained it in the very first sentence and I had read over it, just like many people read over the error that you found in the first sentence of the book. Nice one! I wonder what the "Infinitely" was replaced with - probably not "Finitely" :) I had…

cards.title: FDA may allow some toxic chemicals to be added to food without safety review

depth.text: the FDA may let **some toxic chemicals** go straight into food **without a safety review**

The current **threshold of regulation** exemption covers chemicals in food-contact materials below 0.5 parts per billion if they aren’t carcinogenic; the proposal would extend it to chemicals added directly as ingredients. Advocates say the rule misses **cumulative effects**, pointing to FDA data showing more kids’ cereal samples contained perchlorate after a 2005 exemption.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say poorly studied chemicals do not belong in food; others question whether the article’s examples show meaningful harm.

comments.text: I posted this because I thought it both interesting and troubling to see the disconnect between RFK Jr's stated goals and values and his actions in practice. Like many out there, I connected with some of the underlying messages and values that his campaign put forward. However, the more I learn about him and his past, the more I question not just his methods and expertise, but his truthfulness…

"generally regarded as safe” (Gras)

No matter what you may argue about whether or not these specific chemicals are safe at the contaminant dosage, we do not NEED more poorly studied chemicals present in our environment.

cards.title: Mxc: Microsoft Execution Containers version 1.0.0

depth.text: Microsoft is making **execution containers** generally available to limit what **AI agents** can access

Developers declare **files and network destinations** in a unified JSON configuration, and MXC maps those controls to containers on Windows, macOS, or Linux. **Learning mode** blocks and records ungranted access; **Permissive mode** records access it would have denied but lets it continue.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters call it a welcome first step or useful for enterprises; skeptics say the design is immature, too complex, or unnecessary beside Linux options.

comments.text: I’ve had a good think about this, and while it’s good to see them finally answering bubblewrap, the truth is that we as an industry have been ridiculously at permissioning for some time and this does not solve this. It’s all very well saying we have read only resource access, but then you connect up to JIRA and all of a sudden you’ve got a different identity system, different resource model and…

I'd give it a whirl, but wiped my last windows machine a year ago precisely because stuff like this "just works" on linux. VM, containers, process containment all have matured options and have for years

Sadly, skimming the docs about how the different backends work makes me think that almost this entire project was done by a recent-gen LLM that interpreted its instructions as “make these things work at all costs” instead of “make a considered design that cleanly and securely fits its use case”. Even the bubblewrap integration docs are basically a stream of consciousness vibe splat. I have…

The biggest news - and the most welcome one - is that W11 25H2 August cumulative update now allows anyone to set up App containers without administrative privileges. Then they built mxc on top of that. This is a first step: uncertain, unstable, with many improvements to build upon; but always a step, enabling pioneers out there to explore something new. Thanks for sharing!
What are these people running from? They're not! They're running to the world's toughest competition in town!

cards.title: Nix wrote half of my debugger

depth.text: someone used Nix to build a **debugger** that can **replay and inspect race conditions**

Rewind VM reruns a Nix build under **different thread schedules** and narrows the first failure to **one step**. Its app can show source and stack frames, compare two runs, and open gdb at the playhead without changing the recording.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters want to move more work into Nix builds to avoid handling cache invalidation themselves; another asks what Nix adds to something that seems to reimplement rr.

comments.text: There is likely a mass of devs that is probably, hmmm, 10x the number of Nix devs from over a year ago, who know exactly what Nix offers and why it is cool, but couldn't be bothered to master it until AI came along and basically "solved the problem". So I'd expect AI to rapidly accelerate Nix adoption. Hopefully, because it is amazing.
Seeing Nix these days is such a whiplash experience. We have fully deterministic systems and then we have LLMs. God ;)
I kind of confused what nix has to do with this considering it seems to basically be reimplementing rr?
I find myself moving more and more non-build things into nix builds because I don't want to roll my own cache invalidation. Seems like this is yet another reason to do so.

Dude, this is amazing stuff. Farid really is putting out banger after Nix banger haha. This sounds like a mini/less capable Antithesis runtime, but running on your machine. Curious: how does Rewind deal with randomness?

glossary.computer vision: Software that examines pictures or video to spot and identify what's shown.
glossary.projection mapping: Putting images from a projector onto real surfaces so they line up with things in the room.
glossary.spatial computing: Using computers to place information into the physical spaces around you.
glossary.popovers: Small panels that appear over a page when you tap or click something.
glossary.GPL-3: GNU General Public License version 3: rules for sharing software and changes to it.
glossary.hard paywall: A block that keeps you from reading an article unless you pay or sign in.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.constrained decoding: Making a model choose only from answers it is allowed to give.
glossary.calibration: How well a model’s confidence matches how often its choices are actually right.
glossary.temperature scaling: A way to adjust confidence scores so they better match how often answers are right.
glossary.holdout: A set of examples kept aside to check a model on data it did not train on.
glossary.fine-tuning: Training an already-built model a bit more on examples for a particular job.
glossary.macro F1: A score across answer categories that gives each category equal weight.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.zero-shot classifier: A model asked to sort things into categories without examples for that task.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.S3: An online storage service where files can be kept and read over the internet.
glossary.Parquet: A file format that stores table data grouped by columns, so tools can read the columns they need.
glossary.row group: A block of rows stored together inside a data file.
glossary.async I/O: Asynchronous input/output: fetching data while other work continues, instead of sitting idle waiting.
glossary.AI: Artificial intelligence: computer systems designed to do tasks people associate with thinking.
glossary.parameter: A setting inside an AI model that helps shape what it learns and produces.
glossary.threshold of regulation (TOR): An exemption that lets certain chemicals avoid a safety review when used at very low levels in food-contact materials.
glossary.parts per billion (ppb): A way to describe a tiny amount: one part of a substance for every billion parts of a product.
glossary.hormone disruptors: Chemicals that interfere with the body’s hormone signals.
glossary.GRAS: Generally regarded as safe: a route that has let companies decide ingredients are safe without telling the FDA, according to campaigners.
glossary.emulsifiers: Substances that help ingredients that would normally separate stay mixed together.
glossary.containment: Limiting which files, connections, or other parts of a device a program can access.
glossary.JSON: A common format for storing and sending data in a way that programs can read.
glossary.SDK: Software Development Kit: tools a company provides so people can make apps for its device.
glossary.sandbox: A separate, contained space where software can be tested without affecting the rest of a computer or system.
glossary.least privilege: Giving a program only the access it needs to do its job.
glossary.WSL: Windows Subsystem for Linux: a way to use Linux tools on Windows.
glossary.Nix: A tool for describing a build's inputs so the build can be repeated.
glossary.race condition: When the order of events can cause a program to end up in the wrong state.
glossary.thread schedule: The order in which a computer lets a program's threads take turns running.
glossary.derivation: A Nix build recipe that lists the source and other inputs needed to make a program.
glossary.debug symbols: Extra information that lets a debugger connect a program's running state to its source code.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.deterministic: Something that gives the same result when it gets the same input.
glossary.open model: An AI model shared for others to use, though “open” can mean different things.
glossary.M&A: Mergers and acquisitions: when companies combine or one company buys another.
glossary.acquihiring: Buying a company mainly to bring its employees onto your team.
glossary.compute: The processing power computers use to run AI or other software.
glossary.diffusion model: An image-making AI that starts with visual noise and gradually turns it into a picture.
